Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Deploying a Basic Replica Set
Deploying a Basic Replica Set
Hands-on steps to configure and initialize rs0 for reliable failover.
This lesson focuses on a small, reproducible deployment pattern for development. You will practice creating separate data directories, starting three mongod processes with distinct ports and the same replica set name, initiating the set in the mongo shell, and confirming replication. The setup mirrors production ideas but runs on localhost for learning and troubleshooting.
In this lesson
Start mongod instances — separate ports and dbpaths
Initialize with rs.initiate — define members
Connect app — multi-host connection string
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Example local topology
mongod on localhost:27017 — candidate primary
mongod on localhost:27018 — secondary
mongod on localhost:27019 — secondary
Quick note
Use unique data directories for each instance and the exact same replica set name when starting mongod. This avoids corruption and ensures proper membership.
Key Takeaway
A functional replica set requires separate mongod processes that share the same replica set name, unique dbpaths and ports, and an initiation step so members form a coherent topology discoverable by drivers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure multiple mongod instances to belong to a single replica set, initialize that set from the mongo shell, and add members later as your topology grows. You will learn which mongod startup parameters are essential for replica sets—such as the flag that names the set, the ports and data directories that keep processes separate, and the network bindings that allow members to reach one another. You will also practice building a connection string that lists multiple seed hosts so an application driver can discover the primary and handle failover automatically. Each objective is practical: you will run mongod processes with distinct dbpaths, run rs. initiate with a configuration that lists members by host and id, and use rs. add to expand an existing set. Finally, you’ll verify replication by checking member states and reading from a secondary when appropriate. These skills matter because they make your development environment resilient and help you avoid common configuration errors that block replication or cause data problems.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Learning Objectives — Verification
Verification checklist
  • Create separate data directories and log files for each instance.
  • Start mongod with the same replica set name on distinct ports.
  • Run rs.initiate with members listed by host and integer ids.
  • Use rs.status to confirm one PRIMARY and two SECONDARY states.
  • Insert data on the primary and read from a secondary after enabling reads.
  • Test application connectivity with a connection string that lists seed hosts and replicaSet name.
Common checks
Check that each mongod uses a unique dbpath and that bind_ip allows members to communicate. If logs show connection failures, inspect bind addresses and firewall rules in production.

screens.title: Prepare your environment
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a replica set begins with a disciplined file layout and process separation. Each mongod instance must have its own data directory and log file to prevent interference and data corruption. In practice, you will create three directories for a minimum recommended development replica set. For example, create directories such as /data/db/rs0-0, /data/db/rs0-1, and /data/db/rs0-2. Removing old data before you start helps avoid leftover journal files or index inconsistencies. Use the operating system command to remove any previous directories, then recreate them with appropriate ownership and permissions for the mongod process. A common misconception is that multiple mongod instances can safely share a single dbpath if they run on different ports. That is incorrect and leads to corruption or startup errors. Another frequent mistake is forgetting to create the log path, which makes troubleshooting difficult when a process fails silently. As a concrete example, run a remove command to clean old directories, then mkdir to create fresh ones. The takeaway is simple: unique dbpaths and log paths are non-negotiable for safe multi-instance deployments. What will you check in each log file first after starting mongod?

keyIdea.title: Foundation
keyIdea.text: Unique data directories and log files prevent corruption and make troubleshooting straightforward when running multiple mongod instances.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Prepare your environment
Create and clean directories
Start by removing old data and creating fresh dbpaths for each instance. This avoids leftover files that can block startup.
rm -rf /data/db/rs0-0 /data/db/rs0-1 /data/db/rs0-2
mkdir -p /data/db/rs0-0 /data/db/rs0-1 /data/db/rs0-2
Why this matters
Separate dbpaths prevent multiple mongod processes from corrupting the same files and ensure isolated storage for each member.
Common mistake
Reusing a single dbpath for multiple instances is a serious error and will produce data corruption or startup failures.
Example verification
After creating directories, confirm ownership and list contents. If log files are created when mongod starts, inspect them for binding and replication messages.
Key Takeaway

Always use unique dbpaths and log files before starting multiple mongod instances; this is the most basic safety check.

screens.title: Key mongod startup parameters
screens.narratorSegment: A correct mongod startup command is central to forming a replica set. Each flag has a specific role. The port flag sets the TCP port where the instance listens and must be unique per process on the same host. The dbpath points to the directory that stores data files; it must be unique per instance. The logpath directs process logs to a file for troubleshooting. The replSet flag assigns the replica set name—this name must be identical across all members you intend to group. The fork flag runs the process in the background so your terminal is free; in development it's convenient but not required. The bind_ip flag limits network interfaces the mongod listens on; for local testing use localhost or 127.0.0.1. A common misconception is that omitting bind_ip will always allow inter-node communication; by default many mongod builds bind only to localhost, and being explicit avoids connectivity surprises. For example, starting an instance with its own port, dbpath, and the same replSet name ensures the instance is ready to join the configured set once you initiate. Always double-check that the replSet string you pass at startup exactly matches the id you later use in the initiation command.

keyIdea.title: Startup flags
keyIdea.text: Each startup flag controls an essential resource: port for network, dbpath for storage, logpath for diagnostics, replSet for grouping, fork for backgrounding, and bind_ip for network reachability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Key mongod startup parameters
Startup flags explained
--port
Unique listening port per mongod process.
--dbpath
Directory for data files; must be unique per instance.
--logpath
File for process logs used in troubleshooting.
--replSet
Replica set name that groups members; must match initiation document.
--fork
Run mongod in the background; convenient for multi-process setups.
--bind_ip
Controls network interfaces the process listens on; be explicit in production.
Example command
mongod --port 27017 --dbpath /data/db/rs0-0 --logpath /data/db/rs0-0/mongod.log --replSet rs0 --fork --bind_ip localhost
Watch out

If the replSet name differs between members or the initiation document, the nodes will not form a set. Exact matching is required.

screens.title: Start three mongod instances
screens.narratorSegment: Now we run three mongod instances that will form our replica set. Each command specifies a different port, a distinct dbpath, and the same replSet name. Running them in the background with fork is convenient for a local lab so you can continue using the terminal. A concrete example uses ports 27017, 27018, and 27019 and data directories rs0-0, rs0-1, and rs0-2. After launching each process, check the corresponding log file for a message indicating the process is waiting for connections and for any warnings about binding or data files. If a process fails to start, common culprits are permissions on the dbpath, a port already in use, or accidentally reusing a dbpath. Another gotcha is forgetting to include the replSet flag; a mongod started without that flag will operate as a standalone server and will not participate in initiation. In a production environment you would run these on separate machines for fault isolation, but the commands shown are the exact sequence you can run on a development host to learn the process. What log message will you look for to confirm the instance is ready to join a replica set?

keyIdea.title: Launch commands
keyIdea.text: Start each mongod with a unique port and dbpath while using the same replSet name so all processes are prepared to form a replica set when initiated.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Start three mongod instances
Commands to run
# Instance 1 (primary candidate)
mongod --port 27017 --dbpath /data/db/rs0-0 --logpath /data/db/rs0-0/mongod.log --replSet rs0 --fork --bind_ip localhost

# Instance 2
mongod --port 27018 --dbpath /data/db/rs0-1 --logpath /data/db/rs0-1/mongod.log --replSet rs0 --fork --bind_ip localhost

# Instance 3
mongod --port 27019 --dbpath /data/db/rs0-2 --logpath /data/db/rs0-2/mongod.log --replSet rs0 --fork --bind_ip localhost
After running these commands, you should see three mongod processes and log files created under each dbpath. If a process exits immediately, open its log for an explanatory message.
Checklist
  • Unique dbpath per instance
  • Distinct port per process
  • Same replSet name across all
  • Log files available for inspection
Common mistake

Starting mongod without --replSet leaves it as a standalone server that won't join a replica set.

screens.title: Initiate the replica set with rs.initiate()
screens.narratorSegment: Once all mongod instances are running with the same replica set name, the next step is to form the set using the mongo shell command to initiate a configuration document. You connect to one running instance and run an initiation call that includes the replica set id and a members array where each member has a unique integer id and a host field specified as hostname:port. The id in the initiation document must match the replSet name you used when starting mongod. After initiation you will typically see the shell prompt change to indicate the replica set name and the node role, for example showing that your connected instance has become primary. A concrete example uses the name rs0 and members for localhost on ports 27017, 27018, and 27019. A common misconception is that rs. initiate magically configures networking; it only registers the members and starts the election process. Networking and bind addresses must already allow the nodes to communicate. After running initiation, use rs. status to confirm each member's state. If a member cannot contact others it will show a connectivity error in status and logs.

keyIdea.title: Forming the set
keyIdea.text: Use rs.initiate with a configuration document whose _id matches replSet and whose members array lists each host and unique integer id.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Initiate the replica set with rs.initiate()
Initiation configuration document
rs.initiate({
  _id: "rs0",
  members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "localhost:27017" },
    { _id: 1, host: "localhost:27018" },
    { _id: 2, host: "localhost:27019" }
  ]
});
The replica set _id must match the replSet flag used at mongod startup. The members array lists member ids and host addresses; these are the seeds the initiating node registers.
After initiation
Expect the shell prompt to reflect the replica set name and role. Then run rs.status to inspect each member's state and connectivity.
Key Takeaway

Initiation registers members and starts election; it does not fix network misconfiguration. Ensure bind_ip and connectivity before initiating.

screens.title: Understanding rs.status() and member roles
screens.narratorSegment: After you initiate a replica set, verifying the cluster is essential. The rs. status command returns a document describing each member, its state string, and additional connectivity and replication details. The state string shows whether a member is PRIMARY, SECONDARY, or another state. A clear verification pattern is to expect one primary and the rest secondaries in a three-member set. Look for stateStr fields and member ids that match your initiation document. You can also inspect oplog replication progress and last heartbeat times reported in the status output. A frequent misconception is to assume immediate full replication; secondaries may take short time to sync data and catch up. If you see a member with connectivity errors or a state like STARTUP2, check that the member has access to its data directory and can reach the other hosts; logs often show the underlying mismatch. As a concrete step, run rs. status and confirm three members are listed and that the primary's stateStr is PRIMARY. If replication is delayed, recheck logs and network binding settings. Understanding rs.status() and member roles means use rs.status to confirm roles, connectivity, and replication progress; expect one primary and remaining secondary members in a healthy three-node set.. In practical terms, how to verify primary and secondary states and check member health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Understanding rs.status()
What rs.status shows
  • Member list with ids and host addresses.
  • stateStr fields indicating PRIMARY, SECONDARY, or other states.
  • Heartbeat and replication lag indicators for health checks.
Use this output to confirm your topology and to identify members that cannot reach the set or have not finished initial sync.
Quick check
Run rs.status and look for a single PRIMARY and the expected number of SECONDARY nodes. If a node is missing, inspect its log for connection or permission errors.
Misconception

Do not expect instantaneous replication completion; allow secondaries time to catch up and check oplog progress instead of assuming failure immediately.

screens.title: Adding members with rs.add()
screens.narratorSegment: Replica sets can grow after the initial formation. Use the rs. add command from the mongo shell connected to the replica set to add a new member to an already initialized set. This avoids reinitializing and preserves the existing primary and data. The rs. add call accepts a host string and optional member settings; for simple additions you supply the hostname and port of the new mongod process. A practical example is bringing up an extra mongod on a new machine or port and calling rs. add to register it with the set. A common mistake is attempting to call rs. add before the new mongod is running with the correct replSet name; the mongod must be started with the same replica set name and be reachable by address. In production, prefer using fully qualified names or static IPs for host entries rather than ephemeral or localhost addresses so members resolve consistently. After adding a member, monitor rs. status and the new member's log to ensure it completes initial sync and transitions to SECONDARY. What conditions will you check to confirm the added member is healthy?

keyIdea.title: Expanding safely
keyIdea.text: Use rs.add to register a running mongod that uses the same replica set name; ensure the new node completes initial sync and becomes SECONDARY.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Adding members with rs.add()
rs.add usage
// From the mongo shell connected to the set
rs.add("newhost:27020");
Ensure the new host is running mongod with --replSet set to the same name and that network binding allows connections. Monitor initial sync progress until the member reaches SECONDARY.
Checklist after rs.add
  • New mongod started with same replSet name
  • Network reachable by the existing members
  • rs.status shows the new member and its state
Key Takeaway

rs.add is the supported way to grow a live replica set; verify initial sync and connectivity after adding a member.

screens.title: Connect your application with a multi-host URI
screens.narratorSegment: Connecting an application to a replica set requires a connection string that lists multiple seed hosts and the replica set name. This enables the driver to discover the full topology and find the current primary for writes. Instead of a single host entry, provide a comma-separated list with ports, and include the replicaSet parameter. For example in Node. js you construct a URI that lists localhost on three ports and includes replicaSet equals rs0 and a read preference. A common pitfall is supplying only a single host in the URI. If the driver connects to a host that later becomes secondary or unreachable, it cannot automatically discover the other members and will fail to reconnect reliably. By listing multiple seed hosts, the driver will connect to any reachable member, retrieve the replica set configuration, and direct operations to the proper primary. After connecting, perform a simple insert to verify writes succeed and then close the client. Always test failover by stopping the primary and observing that the driver reconnects to the newly elected primary. How will you validate that your application still writes after a primary failover?

This enables the driver to discover the full topology and find the current primary for writes. keyIdea.title: Driver discovery
keyIdea.text: Use a connection string with multiple seed hosts and the replicaSet name so the driver can discover the topology and handle failover without manual changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Connect your application
Node.js connection example
const { MongoClient } = require('mongodb');
const uri = "mongodb://localhost:27017,localhost:27018,localhost:27019/?replicaSet=rs0&readPreference=primary";
const client = new MongoClient(uri);
// connect, insert a document, then close
This connection string lists three seed hosts and names the replica set. The driver uses this list to discover the current topology and route operations to the primary.
Pitfall
Using a single host in the URI prevents the driver from discovering other members and can break failover behavior.

screens.title: Common deployment mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring errors interfere with replica set deployment. First, reusing the same dbpath for multiple mongod instances is a severe mistake that leads to file corruption or startup failures; always create unique directories. Second, omitting or misconfiguring bind_ip can prevent members from communicating. For development, localhost is fine, but in production use the server’s IP or fully qualified domain name. Third, providing a single host in your application connection string prevents the driver from discovering other members and disables automatic failover. Contrast a multi-host URI that lists seed hosts and a replicaSet name with the single-host URI that cannot adapt to a primary change. Another subtle issue is mismatched replica set names between startup flags and initiation documents; they must be identical. For each mistake we recommend a specific check: confirm dbpaths are different, inspect log files for binding failures, and validate your connection URI lists multiple hosts and replicaSet. In practice, these checks usually surface the root problem quickly and let you fix the deployment without reinitializing the set. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Common deployment mistakes
Mistake: Reused dbpath
Never run multiple mongod processes against the same data directory; it causes corruption and unpredictable behavior.
Mistake: Missing bind_ip
If bind_ip prevents inter-node communication, members will fail to see each other. Be explicit about network interfaces in testing and production.
Mistake: Single-host connection string
A connection URI with only one host cannot enable driver discovery or automatic failover. Use multiple seed hosts and replicaSet parameter.
Bad
mongodb://myhost:27017/mydb
Good
mongodb://host1:27017,host2:27018,host3:27019/?replicaSet=rs0

screens.title: From local lab to production
screens.narratorSegment: While the development pattern uses localhost and multiple ports on one machine, production deployments follow stronger isolation and naming practices. In production, run each mongod on a separate physical or virtual host to maximize fault tolerance. Use fully qualified domain names or static IP addresses in member host entries so nodes resolve consistently across the network; avoid using localhost or ephemeral hostnames for production members. Configure bind_ip to include the server’s IP addresses and ensure network policies allow members to reach each other. Monitoring and backup practices are also important: monitor replication lag and member states so you can respond to long-standing secondary lag or election storms. When adding a new member in production, use rs. add and allow initial sync to complete while watching status output and logs. A typical misconception is that simply copying the local commands to production yields a robust system; in reality, DNS, firewalls, system limits, and storage configuration all matter. Always test failover in a controlled window and ensure your driver connection string lists multiple seed hosts so applications remain resilient when a primary changes. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to deploy a simple three-member MongoDB replica set for development and testing. We will cover the practical steps: creating separate data directories, starting three mongod processes with the same replica set name, initiating the set using the shell command that defines members, and verifying that one node becomes primary while others become secondary. You will also see how to add members to an existing set and how application drivers discover the topology using a connection string with multiple seed hosts. Understanding these steps matters because a replica set provides automatic failover and data redundancy, and correct configuration prevents common deployment errors such as reuse of a data directory or misconfigured network bindings. As a concrete orientation, we’ll use localhost ports 27017, 27018, and 27019 and the replica set name rs0 so you can reproduce the steps on a single machine. Keep an eye out for typical mistakes like missing bind addresses or identical dbpaths. By the end, you’ll be able to start a three-member replica set and connect a simple application that tolerates a primary failure. What will you check first when you start the mongod processes?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure multiple mongod instances to belong to a single replica set, initialize that set from the mongo shell, and add members later as your topology grows. You will learn which mongod startup parameters are essential for replica sets—such as the flag that names the set, the ports and data directories that keep processes separate, and the network bindings that allow members to reach one another. You will also practice building a connection string that lists multiple seed hosts so an application driver can discover the primary and handle failover automatically. Each objective is practical: you will run mongod processes with distinct dbpaths, run rs. initiate with a configuration that lists members by host and id, and use rs. add to expand an existing set. Finally, you’ll verify replication by checking member states and reading from a secondary when appropriate. These skills matter because they make your development environment resilient and help you avoid common configuration errors that block replication or cause data problems.

This second objectives slide clarifies the verification steps you will perform to demonstrate each skill. You will create clean data directories, start three mongod instances on different ports, and confirm that each process wrote its own log file. You will then initiate the replica set with a configuration document that lists members by host and integer id and observe the election that makes one node primary. To verify replication you will insert a document on the primary and then connect to a secondary and allow reads from it to confirm the data replicated. You should also practice rs. status to inspect state strings and member roles. Finally, you will compose and test a driver connection string that specifies multiple seed hosts and the replica set name, observing that the driver discovers the topology and connects to the primary. These verifications are practical proofs that your configuration is correct and that the replica set behaves as expected under simple read and write operations.

Setting up a replica set begins with a disciplined file layout and process separation. Each mongod instance must have its own data directory and log file to prevent interference and data corruption. In practice, you will create three directories for a minimum recommended development replica set. For example, create directories such as /data/db/rs0-0, /data/db/rs0-1, and /data/db/rs0-2. Removing old data before you start helps avoid leftover journal files or index inconsistencies. Use the operating system command to remove any previous directories, then recreate them with appropriate ownership and permissions for the mongod process. A common misconception is that multiple mongod instances can safely share a single dbpath if they run on different ports. That is incorrect and leads to corruption or startup errors. Another frequent mistake is forgetting to create the log path, which makes troubleshooting difficult when a process fails silently. As a concrete example, run a remove command to clean old directories, then mkdir to create fresh ones. The takeaway is simple: unique dbpaths and log paths are non-negotiable for safe multi-instance deployments. What will you check in each log file first after starting mongod?

A correct mongod startup command is central to forming a replica set. Each flag has a specific role. The port flag sets the TCP port where the instance listens and must be unique per process on the same host. The dbpath points to the directory that stores data files; it must be unique per instance. The logpath directs process logs to a file for troubleshooting. The replSet flag assigns the replica set name—this name must be identical across all members you intend to group. The fork flag runs the process in the background so your terminal is free; in development it's convenient but not required. The bind_ip flag limits network interfaces the mongod listens on; for local testing use localhost or 127.0.0.1. A common misconception is that omitting bind_ip will always allow inter-node communication; by default many mongod builds bind only to localhost, and being explicit avoids connectivity surprises. For example, starting an instance with its own port, dbpath, and the same replSet name ensures the instance is ready to join the configured set once you initiate. Always double-check that the replSet string you pass at startup exactly matches the id you later use in the initiation command.

Now we run three mongod instances that will form our replica set. Each command specifies a different port, a distinct dbpath, and the same replSet name. Running them in the background with fork is convenient for a local lab so you can continue using the terminal. A concrete example uses ports 27017, 27018, and 27019 and data directories rs0-0, rs0-1, and rs0-2. After launching each process, check the corresponding log file for a message indicating the process is waiting for connections and for any warnings about binding or data files. If a process fails to start, common culprits are permissions on the dbpath, a port already in use, or accidentally reusing a dbpath. Another gotcha is forgetting to include the replSet flag; a mongod started without that flag will operate as a standalone server and will not participate in initiation. In a production environment you would run these on separate machines for fault isolation, but the commands shown are the exact sequence you can run on a development host to learn the process. What log message will you look for to confirm the instance is ready to join a replica set?

Once all mongod instances are running with the same replica set name, the next step is to form the set using the mongo shell command to initiate a configuration document. You connect to one running instance and run an initiation call that includes the replica set id and a members array where each member has a unique integer id and a host field specified as hostname:port. The id in the initiation document must match the replSet name you used when starting mongod. After initiation you will typically see the shell prompt change to indicate the replica set name and the node role, for example showing that your connected instance has become primary. A concrete example uses the name rs0 and members for localhost on ports 27017, 27018, and 27019. A common misconception is that rs. initiate magically configures networking; it only registers the members and starts the election process. Networking and bind addresses must already allow the nodes to communicate. After running initiation, use rs. status to confirm each member's state. If a member cannot contact others it will show a connectivity error in status and logs.

After you initiate a replica set, verifying the cluster is essential. The rs. status command returns a document describing each member, its state string, and additional connectivity and replication details. The state string shows whether a member is PRIMARY, SECONDARY, or another state. A clear verification pattern is to expect one primary and the rest secondaries in a three-member set. Look for stateStr fields and member ids that match your initiation document. You can also inspect oplog replication progress and last heartbeat times reported in the status output. A frequent misconception is to assume immediate full replication; secondaries may take short time to sync data and catch up. If you see a member with connectivity errors or a state like STARTUP2, check that the member has access to its data directory and can reach the other hosts; logs often show the underlying mismatch. As a concrete step, run rs. status and confirm three members are listed and that the primary's stateStr is PRIMARY. If replication is delayed, recheck logs and network binding settings. Understanding rs.status() and member roles means use rs.status to confirm roles, connectivity, and replication progress; expect one primary and remaining secondary members in a healthy three-node set.. In practical terms, how to verify primary and secondary states and check member health. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Replica sets can grow after the initial formation. Use the rs. add command from the mongo shell connected to the replica set to add a new member to an already initialized set. This avoids reinitializing and preserves the existing primary and data. The rs. add call accepts a host string and optional member settings; for simple additions you supply the hostname and port of the new mongod process. A practical example is bringing up an extra mongod on a new machine or port and calling rs. add to register it with the set. A common mistake is attempting to call rs. add before the new mongod is running with the correct replSet name; the mongod must be started with the same replica set name and be reachable by address. In production, prefer using fully qualified names or static IPs for host entries rather than ephemeral or localhost addresses so members resolve consistently. After adding a member, monitor rs. status and the new member's log to ensure it completes initial sync and transitions to SECONDARY. What conditions will you check to confirm the added member is healthy?

Connecting an application to a replica set requires a connection string that lists multiple seed hosts and the replica set name. This enables the driver to discover the full topology and find the current primary for writes. Instead of a single host entry, provide a comma-separated list with ports, and include the replicaSet parameter. For example in Node. js you construct a URI that lists localhost on three ports and includes replicaSet equals rs0 and a read preference. A common pitfall is supplying only a single host in the URI. If the driver connects to a host that later becomes secondary or unreachable, it cannot automatically discover the other members and will fail to reconnect reliably. By listing multiple seed hosts, the driver will connect to any reachable member, retrieve the replica set configuration, and direct operations to the proper primary. After connecting, perform a simple insert to verify writes succeed and then close the client. Always test failover by stopping the primary and observing that the driver reconnects to the newly elected primary. How will you validate that your application still writes after a primary failover?
